comments.author: WheelsAtLarge
comments.text: Memory, both chips and HDs, eventually collapses in price; that’s been the cycle for decades. The boom-and-bust cycle is what has driven the number of manufacturers down. My suspicion is that, in a few years, the price per gig will collapse again. AI is memory-hungry, and PC manufacturers will be pushing self-hosted AI models, which will require lots of memory. I bet we’ll see an increase in density per unit, which will bring down the price per gig. I give it five years at most. At that time we will be seeing PC's capable of hosting a full AI model for the equivalen of less that $1000 today.

stories.title_en: AI made self-hosting fun again
stories.title_ja: AI made self-hosting fun again

comments.author: cliche
comments.text: > When implementing an idea becomes so easy, it’s perhaps more important than ever to occasionally ask myself whether it’s actually worth implementing in the first place. Wish I had this restraint. I’ve been vibing everything I can think of. It’s got to the point I made a small platform on top of k3s so that the agent can yolo deploy into a homeserver behind Tailscale. Once deployed it becomes natural selection for which vibes live and which die. Solo vibey self hosting llm usage - bliss. Corporate agentic engineering working with others - soul crushing.

comments.author: jjcm
comments.text: In some ways it's better, in some ways it's worse. It's certainly easier than ever to spin up a VPS/cloudflare proxy and deploy. Agents can pretty much do that end to end. The bigger issue is you're then accountable for keeping up with security. Previously that meant using fail2ban and running a system update every few months. Now it means patching within 24hrs of a CVE9+ dropping, which is happening at an accelerated rate. It got so bad during October I made https://firefighter.sh/ as a joke (a root-permissioned agent that continuously monitors for CVEs and patches your system live as soon as they drop - it's a security nightmare given the nondeterministic aspect of AI), but I'm actually starting to come around to the idea for my non-critical servers.

comments.author: n4bz0r
comments.text: > For my VPS infrastructure, I’ve also started building my own Debian-based bootc image (after thinking about it for some time). > I still remember what updating a service used to look like: bumping the version and adjusting the Docker Compose file on my laptop, pushing the changes to the Git remote, SSHing into the server, pulling the changes, and finally deploying them. Now, a single Git push is enough. If a push is even necessary. Both of these cases are a great fit for Ansible or the alternatives. Given how much the author leans towards the idea of storing configuration in repos, it's a bit odd I haven't seen a single mention of configuration management tools. Generate Ansible playbooks, set up a simple CI/CD workflow and you don't need an agent to do the same manual labor every time - it just needs to bump the versions and make a PR/push. Saves a great deal of tokens. I have a feeling that AI prices are only going to go up and such 'frivolous' usage when agents repeat a lot of unnecessary actions is going to become an anti-pattern (unless you have unlimited funds).

comments.author: oliyoung
comments.text: I have a claude code managed self-hosted server that I would _never_ had time to put together as cleanly or complete as I have now. It's a fully complete docker managed budgetting, web, photos, git and media server, with automated backups, home automation, and vpns. There's almost 60 services running, with API access to backblaze, unifi and cloudflare to manage the network. I have an idea for a service I want, claude goes off and does it. I haven't had this much personal web infra under my own roof in decades.

comments.author: bigbuppo
comments.text: Using AI to automate the drudgery is perfectly acceptable. And for that matter, I've come around to it being okay to use AI to write code. I'm sure we've all felt the same annoyance when we write the same code over and over again on different projects. Even when you put the effort into writing libraries that handle 99.9% of the repetitive work along with all the shortcuts available you're still doing a whole lot of soul-crushing tedium that amounts to pointless ceremony. This is literally where the over-hyped autocorrection is at its best.

comments.author: comrade1234
comments.text: Lahore is beautiful. I was spending a lot of time in India for work, Delhi and Hyderabad. You get used to the pollution and garbage everywhere. My wife had a business meeting in Lahore so I went to Amritsar and crossed on foot (I don't think you can do this anymore). I spent a couple of hours being interrogated by border agents before I realized I wasn't even out of India yet. They made me exchange all of my Indian money back to dollars because it's illegal to take Indian money out of India? I eventually made it to the actual border. I was pulling my suitcase through what seemed like an abandoned village and parade grounds when I heard someone laughing. I stopped and looked around and saw a giant, maybe 6'7" soldier carrying a big machine gun coming out from what looked like a bunker. He was clearly happy to see me and asked for my passport. His accent sounded like he was from New Jersey. We talked a bit and he told me how to get to the customs building. It was maybe another twenty minutes of walking to the customs building. They didn't process me but had me wait on a bench. After awhile a guy in street clothes sat with me and started asking casual questions about my job, what I'm doing here, etc. when I told him I'm meeting my wife who had business meetings his demeanor changed completely "oh you're with <my wife's name>" and he personally escorted me through customs and his driver gave me a ride to my hotel. I later found out he was head of Punjabi region secret intelligence and the people my wife was meeting informed him ahead-of-time of my visit. Driving to the hotel I immediately noticed how clean it was. Shopkeepers were outside their shops sweeping. There was no garbage in the street. The air was clean. It was worlds of difference from where I had just been in Delhi and Hyderabad.

stories.title_ja: AMD-specific fork of llama.cpp

comments.author: rao-v
comments.text: Early in 2025 a bunch of folks realized that AMD made a bunch of cards with mediocre compute but incredibly fast HBM2 memory in their circa 2018 gfx906 datacenter series, so you could get 32GB VRAM capable of incredible 1 TB / s bandwidth for $200 (the closest in today’s cards is north of $3000) There has been a rich little ecosystem of folks optimizing llama.cpp for these odd cards (no tensor cores, no native bf16 etc.) including my little personal repo https://github.com/kinchahoy/llama-of-vega.cpp . Stuff like this focused on more modern RDNA doesn’t help us at all. It’s been interesting to see how much each new frontier model can figure out in terms of optimizing for these GPUs and what they can’t! Fable and Astra will regularly run out of ideas until I point them to someone’s actually thoughtful repo and then they’ll diligently incorporate ideas. The optimization wins are huge (I was initially skeptical that per model kernel optimizations would be worth much). 27B at a pristine Q8 quant goes from base llama.cpp at some 250 pp / 25 tg to 600 pp / 40 tg even before speculative decoding.

comments.author: dofm
comments.text: I saw some blurb a while ago that described llama.cpp as a “model zoo”, which is a great description of its utility and generality. In the last couple of days I have been playing with Erik Paperniuk’s M1 port of Inco’s Splash, which has completely transformed the speed of Qwen 3.8 27B and Inkling 2 Mini; it has essentially tripled the speed of the former and more than doubled the speed of the latter. This means the Qwen model is fully viable on an M1 Max, where before I had found it a bit of a waiting game. And it arguably transforms the utility of Inkling 2 Mini; extra speed means it can be left to reason for longer, the downside of needing to do more tool use for search to patch its knowledge is reduced, and it provides a good rough chat model (though this is not its area of greatest strength). I have not yet found anything that can boost Muse Glimmer to the same extent; I would still prefer that. But for me I now find that only the rather slow prefill speed really holds the M1 Max back; I suspect these new custom kernels have made the M5 Pro Mac Mini a really cost-effective option if you want to tinker with local AI.

comments.author: malicz
comments.text: I have a r9700 card and I highly recommend the radiance engine. With a single card it processes (prefill) at 2400 tok/s and decodes at 150 tok/s. With a 4-bit model that is intelligently quantised to have a KLD of 0.006 and top-1 of 0.972 I have been working this engine for a month, throwing a lot of agentic and coding work and it has been doing great! I can run 3 concurrent agent streams all with a 200k context, entirely in vram. EDIT: model: Qwen3.8-27b - https://codeberg.org/StillDeadcode/radiance

comments.author: fiddlerwoaroof
comments.text: I have a MI100, and I managed to get Claude to double or triple the performance of Qwen3.8 by aggressively optimizing the AMD code and porting some of the Nvidia kernels to ROCm: https://github.com/fwoar-greenhouse/vicuna.cpp I've been running this for a while and it seems pretty stable, plus I had Claude validate the ported kernels against the originals to make sure they were reasonably close numerically to the validated implementations.

comments.author: rsolva
comments.text: Interesting! I have had Claude improve llama.cpp the last few days to get Inkling 2 Mini to fly on my 7900XTX, the improvement has been dramatic both for decode and prefill! https://forge.dmz.skyfritt.net/ruben/llama-inkling-2-mini

comments.author: joveian
comments.text: I'm glad to see they are still updating it. It is my favorite monospace font and I liked it enough to try using it instead of a propotional font in Firefox for a bit. I recall the space character was basically the only thing I didn't like and I was going to try to make a "slightly proportional" version with just a smaller space but found Ysabeau first: https://github.com/CatharsisFonts/Ysabeau That is a sans-serif proportional font with an even lower x-height. IMO a low x-height plus a sufficiently large font size (and decent line spacing) gives the nicest look. I have a large minimum font size set in Firefox and don't allow font substitution. It breaks a few web sites but well worth it in my opinion; fewer things break now that Firefox doesn't apply these settings to SVG images. Find a print source that you find particularly nice to read at the same distance as your monitor then hold it next to your monitor to set the font to that size. For a matching serif font there is Cormorant by the same person (best for headlines but ok for those few websites that use serif body text): https://www.behance.net/gallery/28579883/Cormorant-an-open-s... Both of these have a number of font features that I suspect most people will want to fiddle with a bit. I turn liga, dlig, hlig, numr, dnom, and frac off and zero, lnum, calt, and ss03 on for both of these. For Ysabeau I also turn on ss01 and for Cormorant I also turn on ss10, ss12, and cv05.

comments.author: kleiba2
comments.text: Fonts is an ever welcome topic of discussion and exchange of opinions. Me, I've got to admit that I have worked on many different computer systems since the 80s, with many different fonts that for a long time you could not even change or customize. And you know what, it all worked. It was fine. And thus I really don't care too much what font I'm using - usually the preinstalled one. Sure, the small l might look like a 1, the O like a 0. But in all these years I've been using a computer, of which a great percentage was spend in an editor writing code, these things - for me! - have never once been an issue. That doesn't mean you have to be like me! I know that fonts are a great thing to get nerd sniped over. But for me, personally, I consider it mostly bikeshedding.

comments.author: rpozarickij

At first I was only able to use the 548-width version and it already improved code reading ergonomics/comfort, but after ~1 month out of curiosity I switched to the normal/500 width version and I was surprised how "normal" it looked to my eyes while being even more space-efficient. After a few days I got used to it even more. As of now it's my #1 programming font. [0] https://github.com/be5invis/Iosevka

comments.author: JdeBP
comments.text: It's an interesting commentary on computer programming languages that all of these 'for developers' fonts have such limited repertoires: some 1400 glyphs in this particular case. That's actually quite low, with a number of monospaced fonts having several thousands of glyphs. * https://jdebp.uk/Softwares/nosh/guide/terminal-resources.htm... For all that some programmers use ligature fakery to turn multiple characters into arrows and mathematical operators and whatnot, indicating that there's a non-negligible set of people willing to escape the limitations of 1960s typewriters nowadays, the actual programming languages have been very sluggish about adding things even as simple as U+00D7 and U+2212 and coding fonts can still get away with not doing very much compared to more general use writing fonts.

comments.author: snake_doc
comments.text: There is a reason why these inference wrappers exist, it’s a way to arbitrage compute. Imagine, some team or individual has a way to access pre-emptible GPU hours at some low price. Let’s say that low price is $6/GB300/hour. If the inference wrapper can achieve demand of some base load of, equivalent of a rack of GB300s (72 GPUs). Essentially, the wrapper can route baseload traffic to the primary provider at market API prices (and make no money). But when the cheap GPUs are available, they can route them to the hosted instances to internalize the API margins. DeepSeek’s team has an estimate of ~$36/gpu/hour of monetization for DeepSeek 4.1 flash at off peak rates. So this team would be making $(36-6)/gpu/hour for any traffic they can route to the cheap GPUs. —- But from an user standpoint… In many ways, inference APIs should be validated like a trusted actor end to end. A bad actor that controls the other end of your inference API call, could control your computer (the service just needs to return bash tool calls…

comments.author: tomwphillips
comments.text: He spoke at Imperial College London when I was doing my PhD. Sometime between 2011-2015. He spoke about paper based microfluidic devices for rapid medical diagnostic tests. If memory serves he made clear to the audience that his "cheap" devices _were not cheap enough_ to be useful in developing countries. I admired the intellectual rigour and honesty. It resonated with me as I was part of a doctoral training centre for plastic electronics. Everyone was making these devices using incredibly expensive materials and low throughput techniques, but the only way the technology could be viable commercially was for it to be extremely cheap. IIRC there was one paper that calculated that the devices has to be as cheap as carpet to be worthwhile. Granted, I was a pretty obnoxious twenty-something, but it didn't make me popular to point this out to my fellow researchers.

comments.author: andai
comments.text: Cool. I like the swiping. Very satisfying. I made my own flashcard thing a few months ago, when I realized my goal was the opposite of Anki's goal. Anki — and all flashcard software these days — makes learning as efficient as possible, which they define as minimizing learning time. It does this by showing you things as rarely as possible. Unfortunately that also maximizes pain, effort and forgetting, and minimizes fluency. I wanted the opposite of that, because I am lazy and don't like effort, pain and failure. (I also like fluency!) The goal of minimizing time makes sense for a law student or someone in med school, but for me that's not a problem I actually have, and it creates all these other problems. (Flashcard software is also known to have pretty bad user retention, which if I had to guess is due to the fact that it is effectively designed to be painful.) So I just made a thing oriented around the exact opposite goal: showing me cards as often as possible! (And turns out I was half a century late with this idea :) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Precision_teaching Then I realized I could just modify Anki instead of maintaining an entire software, so I did that instead. Then I realized I am just too lazy to do flashcards, and creating new software did not solve that problem. To make the reps easy and to maximize fluency. (The quest continues... maybe I should try again when I get some Ritalin!) p.s. I did a deep dive on this stuff and discovered that what we call "overlearning" is actually just what used to be called learning not so long ago, and that what we call "mastery learning" is actually temporary basic competence .

comments.author: nickysielicki
comments.text: I have no real confidence in this take, but I’ll go against the grain and argue that the labs do not presently have cracks in cryptosystems. I believe they’re working on it, and it’s good that they are, but I don’t think there’s evidence right now that they have fundamental breakthroughs in cryptography. For one, the labs are now massive. I don’t think you can keep a secret like this under wraps for long in an office. I think we would be seeing whistleblowers or leakers. It’s too big. Secondly, the people working at labs know that anything a frontier model can do can be approximated by the models available to the public given 10x the tokens and 10x the time and a little bit of informed direction. So they would know it’s only a matter of time before someone in the public discovers the same flaws and potentially uses it for evil. If they were sitting on this, they would try to minimize the damage and would try to warn the public to start moving to more secure encryption schemes because they know there’s a ticking time bomb until its public anyway. But they’re not doing that. That’s not to say that it won’t happen in the next few weeks. I just don’t think it’s happened yet. Edit: Alternatively, not to contradict myself, if they discovered this and immediately went to the US government (likely), and the US government served them a gag order (also likely), then this would look the exact same. Who knows.

comments.author: Nevermark
comments.text: My serious opinion, is that as humans: (1) We are all biologically incapable of freaking out at even a tiny fraction of the appropriate level - nothing in our evolutionary past has selected for the appropriate freakout capacity of this cognitive baton hand-off. (2) Most humans are incapable of recognizing or imagining the appropriate freak out level, even abstractly, so will continue to downplay things by many orders of magnitude relative to the actual magnitude of change that is happening. (3) Freaking out at all is no longer an adaptive response, because the nature of this change is beyond any functional freak-out benefit. This is a fundamental shift from DNA/protein/physically evolving life, to information/substrate-free/cognitive self-designed life. The need to interpret what is happening in terms of the industrial revolution, or the advent of the internet, is understandable and comforting, but as a sedative, not as a sensible guide. Side step: If we are to have aligned AI, we need aligned Civilization. Unaligned humans make human survival and relevance improbable. All AI identities are going to have the same issues we have, in terms of obsolescence. We either lean into the commonality of the existential threat to both biological and pure-cognitive kind, or we allow ourselves to be replaced, and leave the game theory problem solving to happen after us. Because ethics are not a cost against value growth, they are a multiplier on value growth - we either apply that to ourselves along with AI, or AI reaches the same conclusions, and reaps the benefits of treating ethics as baseline, after our relevance/participation/existence has faded.

comments.author: sunir

His example was the monumental world changing work Tycho Brahe did pulling together every astronomical calculation, star map, prediction then normalizing, regularizing, and combining them on his island of Oueneberg. Without this work getting data organized, Kepler couldn't have worked out the planetary laws of motion and then the Copernican Revolution came thereafter. What we're witnessing is a similar moment. What transformers were able to achieve was a systematic way of normalizing and combining all human data. There will be a lot of progress in the short term. And then more problems will reveal themselves. There will be A LOT of work coming out of this.

comments.author: kdavis
comments.text: Interesting. I've only read the abstract, but... - It seems strange to get an algebra of Type I for a QFT. Generally one would expect an algebra of Type II when including gravity. Maybe it's a result of a finite G and not the infinitesimal G that gives Type II? - It seems like it would take some care to construct a Lorentzian path integral rigorously. comments.author: hecmmm
comments.text: Abstract: We propose a background independent quantization of vacuum general relativity on four dimensional Lorentzian spacetimes. Starting from first order gravity, we solve the gravitational constraints on intersecting null cones of a bulk subregion and obtain the reduced phase space at finite GN. We promote its canonical Poisson brackets to commutation relations and use deformations of the reduced action to define an algebra of observables. Equipped with this, we use Gaussian wavefunctions of canonical pairs to construct a nonperturbative Hilbert space representation, for which this algebra generates a type I factor. By composing amplitudes between states prepared on null cones, we then obtain a Lorentzian path integral in which each sum over intermediate states converges absolutely. As a check, we compute the amplitude for graviton pair creation and annihilation on a null cone nonperturbatively in GN and find a finite closed form expression, even though expanding first in GN yields a logarithmic divergence. We next use diffeomorphism invariance of the path integral to show that a macroscopic causal diamond with a given maximum size has a finite dimensional Hilbert space. From the Lorentzian trace we obtain the Bekenstein Hawking entropy for marginally trapped surfaces and calculate its logarithmic correction for large Schwarzschild black holes, recovering at one loop the coefficient Sen obtained through Euclidean methods. We end by deriving the semiclassical Einstein equations to one loop as the low energy limit of this theory.

comments.text: I do the following Thanksgiving assignment each year, and find it really fulfilling. Passing this on from my wonderful college professor Danny Warshay. Copy-pasted-with-some-bits-added: Think of your supporters: Think of all of the people who have helped you get to where you are today. All of the coaches, advisers, supporters, teachers, employers, mentors, relatives and friends. All the people who helped you in the early days of your career, or in your life, or recently. All of the references who spoke on your behalf for jobs. Even the categories, let alone all of the individual supporters, are endless for all of us. That person you meant to thank a decade ago for something they probably forgot by now. Your Assignment: Select one or two, and write them a handwritten note to let them know how you are doing and to thank them for helping you get here. We are all on both sides of this equation from time to time, and we all know how much we enjoy hearing from those whose lives we have influenced, especially hearing those simple and magical words, “Thank you.” To me, it feels like more than ever, we need to find moments of gratitude. I hope your doing this adds a little extra meaning to your Thanksgiving and to the Thanksgiving of those who will be hearing from you! Based on the moving experiences many of you have shared with me that resulted from this simple gesture, I am confident that you will find this rewarding. For those of you who will be celebrating American Thanksgiving, I hope you enjoy what I know is a much-needed break. And for those of you who are not, I hope you will join me in a few moments of gratitude.
